items.titel: European troops set to train in Poland for postwar Ukraine deployment
items.anriss: KYIV, Ukraine — Thousands of European troops will gather in Poland next week for the Coalition of the Willing’s first major military exercise, a rehearsal for deploying a multinational force to Ukraine once the war with Russia comes to an …

absaetze.t: KYIV, Ukraine — Thousands of European troops will gather in Poland next week for the Coalition of the Willing’s first major military exercise, a rehearsal for deploying a multinational force to Ukraine once the war with Russia comes to an end, European officials announced this week.

The exercise comes as U.S., Russian and Ukrainian negotiators are set to meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11, special envoy Steve Witkoff said Monday. The meeting caps a tumultuous year for Ukraine’s peace talks, which stalled after the U.S. and Israel began striking Iran in February and revived only in September, when Witkoff and fellow envoy Jared Kushner met Putin in Moscow before traveling to Kyiv for their first visit as negotiators.

Britain and France will jointly lead KOALICJA 26.2 from Nov. 9 to 22, bringing together 2,800 troops from 11 nations for coordinated activities in Poland, France and Turkey under the coalition’s military arm, the Multinational Force-Ukraine (MNF-U). American troops will not participate.

The drills will combine air, land and sea forces to “test how to move, protect and supply a force that would help rebuild Ukraine’s Armed Forces once the fighting ends,” according to a British Ministry of Defence statement.
Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, Turkey and Britain are also taking part.

The training will prepare troops for the force’s eventual missions, which could include securing critical infrastructure, training Ukraine’s military, helping protect the skies and clearing mines from the Black Sea, as part of a broader package of security guarantees for Ukraine, according to the French ministry’s statement.

“This exercise shows the UK is stepping up, alongside France and our allies, to prepare for the day peace comes to Ukraine. This isn’t a hypothetical plan; it’s a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops,” British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in the ministry’s release.
The MNF-U will reportedly not have a peacekeeping or ceasefire-monitoring mandate or operate under NATO command. It would move into Ukraine only after a ceasefire and at Kyiv’s request.

Ceasefire monitoring “would be a different task from that of the multinational force, whose aim is different in nature because it is meant to support the Ukrainian army in its ability to be beefed up,” former French Ambassador to Ukraine Gaël Veyssière told Military Times in April.

The drills will also test “command-and-control arrangements for the force” and assess “how different components can integrate and operate effectively as one multinational force,” according to the British release.

Britain is sending 300 personnel, including soldiers from the British Army’s 7th Light Mechanised Brigade, known as the “Desert Rats,” to rehearse logistical movements. Warsaw will manage the movement of MNF-U troops after the war but will not send its own soldiers into Ukraine. Nearly 2,000 Polish soldiers will take part in addition to the foreign forces, the Polish ministry said.

France is sending “hundreds” of troops, including a unit equipped with about 50 “contact drones,” the second of its kind after one deployed to Romania, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Jacques de Montgros’s told lawmakers last month.

Turkey will not send troops to Poland, the French ministry said, but will stand up the MNF-U’s maritime element in Istanbul, “testing arrangements for maritime mine clearance to allow commercial shipping to safely return to Ukraine’s ports,” according to the British release.

“This exercise will show that the Multinational Force-Ukraine is a real, capable, readily deployable force that represents a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine’s long-term stability and security,” said the commander of MNF-U, British Lt. Gen. Tom Bateman.

The exercise announcements do not specify the final size of a force that could deploy to Ukraine, but Britain and France said earlier this year that they were prepared to contribute roughly 5,000 troops each.

Even a minimal “tripwire” presence would require 10,000 to 25,000 troops, the Center for Strategic and International Studies assessed last year. Because only a third of any force is frontline-ready at a given time, rotations push that number far higher, Ed Arnold, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute and a former British military officer, told Military Times.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has rejected allowing a foreign troop presence in Ukraine, and he warned in September 2025 that Western forces deployed there would be legitimate targets.
Although the MNF-U is not a peacekeeping force, Polish defense officials said its presence is meant to ease Ukrainian fears of a renewed Russian attack once the war ends.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pressed allies on Wednesday to move quickly, pointing out that Russian forces continue to batter Ukraine’s power grid and other critical infrastructure as the country braces for its fifth winter of full-scale war.
“Peace has no alternative, and postwar security guarantees must be truly cast-iron,” he said.

items.titel: From topless joggers to North America’s best grocery shop, a whistle-stop tour casts cities in a new light
items.anriss: Konnichiwa from Fukuoka. I’m on day 13 of this round-the-world tour and you couldn’t ask for a softer landing than Japan’s biggest southern city. It’s a perfect autumn evening, hovering at 14C – there’s a gentle breeze and the city’s bars …

absaetze.t: Konnichiwa from Fukuoka. I’m on day 13 of this round-the-world tour and you couldn’t ask for a softer landing than Japan’s biggest southern city. It’s a perfect autumn evening, hovering at 14C – there’s a gentle breeze and the city’s bars and bistros are glowing with pizza ovens and open grills, while gentle lighting frames diners along bustling boulevards and cosy side streets. As it’s Saturday evening here and this column needs to be filed in time to hit New Zealand in the coming hours, let’s pick up where I left off last Saturday.

A British Airways A350-1000, Heathrow to AustinI haven’t been on BA for nearly a decade, I reckon, and my flight to Texas confirmed why. I am not a disinfecting hygiene freak but so much had spilled and caked onto every surface around my seat that I had to find some disinfecting wipes from Matsumoto Kyoshi and give everything a good scrub. The airline is unique as the cabin crew have their own accent that is hard to pinpoint: 30 per cent camp, 10 per cent wannabe posh, 25 per cent daytime television and a mix of huffs, eye rolls and disappearing acts. From the cockpit, it’s a whole different story, however: perfect vowels, clipped clarity and smooth reassurance. A bit of a relaunch has been announced for the carrier but a deep clean would be a better investment in the immediate term.

Austin – part oneI’ve been to Houston and Dallas many times but Austin only once and it wasn’t memorable. Last Saturday that all changed. I checked into the super buzzy Proper Hotel, dined at the tasty Hestia, was invited to Elon Musk’s Halloween party and went to my room smelling as though I had been chargrilled.

Austin – part twoI woke up Sunday morning and decided on a little trot through town. At 07.00 it was about 22C and I made my way to the river, passing a fit jogger in shorts and no top. It was a guy, I might add. A woman in Lululemon passed on my left and then, around the bend, came another guy without a top. And then another and another. If it were 30C, it would have made sense. If they all had killer bods it would have been even more on the mark but it was neither. Anyway, topless trotting is a thing in Texas’s state capital and I didn’t follow the locals’ lead.

Austin – part threeI’m not big on hard hat tours but I happily obliged when I was offered a tour of Herzog & de Meuron’s new project dubbed Sixth & Blanco. Masterminded by hospitality and retail clever clogs Larry McGuire, the new development builds on his Westside enclave up the street and his surrounding ventures along Sixth. Still nine months from completion, it will surely be the best mixed-use project in North America when it throws open its doors with a small hotel, an array of cafés and restaurants, a private members’ club and cluster of residences on top. Low-slung, woody and concrete, it’s a whole new design language for US retail and hospitality and, a week later, I’m still thinking about how sharp it’s going to be.

Austin – part fourI’ll admit it. I had a “I could live here” moment after walking the aisles of Central Market grocery shop. It is perhaps the best food retailer in North America and must be in the global top five. I loved my Casa Santa Luzia moment in São Paulo a few weeks ago but this is on a different level in terms of scale and offer. There are branches in other parts of the state but it is truly worth a visit if you get off on people who know good grocery. And while we’re offering up big Texan praise, First Light Books and magazine shop Tomo Mags are world class.
Over the north PacificThe Cathay flight from Dallas to Hong Kong is freaking long but I slept for 12 of the 16-plus hours without any chemical support.

ManilaWhere to start after a 13-year absence? It was a treat to be back in the lush and bustling Makati district. Super fun to get a full 30 minutes of airtime on morning show Headstart with Karen Davila asking the questions. Magical for me and my colleagues to be hosted by a Monocle patron in his modernist compound. And long overdue to spend an evening with our fun, chic and charming subscribers. Salamat, Manila. We will be back very soon! There is much to do.

Hong KongIt was too hot for early November for starters but efficient as ever on the business front. Carlyle & Co adds a layer of attentive care to a brisk business trip and its fried HK beef-noodle dish is all the fuel that you need to power on as Europe wakes up and keeps the business day rolling well past midnight.

FukuokaIt’s time to wrap and head out for dinner. I am accompanied by two colleagues and we’re armed with a good restaurant to get rolling and a few drinks to round out the evening. Will report back next Sunday. Have a good week.

items.titel: "La Gradiva" de Marine Atlan reçoit le Reflet d'Or du Geneva International Film Festival
items.anriss: Le Geneva International Film Festival (GIFF) a décerné le Reflet d'Or du meilleur long métrage à "La Gradiva", de la réalisatrice française Marine Atlan. Le Reflet d'Or de la meilleure expérience immersive est attribué à deux Suisses, le …

absaetze.t: Le Geneva International Film Festival (GIFF) a décerné le Reflet d'Or du meilleur long métrage à "La Gradiva", de la réalisatrice française Marine Atlan. Le Reflet d'Or de la meilleure expérience immersive est attribué à deux Suisses, le chorégraphe genevois Gilles Jobin et l'illustrateur zurichois Thomas Ott, pour "Sunset Motel".

"La Gradiva" raconte "avec intensité et justesse" les tumultes de l'âge adolescent, les espoirs et les déceptions d'une jeunesse filmée "avec un naturalisme saisissant, presque mythologique", estime le jury du festival.

Le Reflet d'Or de la meilleure série internationale revient aux Polonais Piotr Derewenda et Wojciech Lepianka pour "Variola Vera", indique samedi soir le GIFF dans un communiqué. La série qui retrace l'émergence d'une épidémie qui a frappé la Pologne dans les années 1960 est "un véritable coup de cœur" du jury.

Le Reflet d'Or de la meilleure expérience immersive est attribué au chorégraphe genevois Gilles Jobin et à l'illustrateur zurichois Thomas Ott pour "Sunset Motel". Le jury souligne l'excellence technologique, la force narrative et la sensibilité poétique de l'œuvre.

Le prix "Future is sensible" va au réalisateur bangladais Abdullah Mohammad Saad pour "Annie", qui a séduit par son minimalisme brut audacieux. "Un seul lieu, une palette de couleurs et une musique sobre, ainsi qu'une caméra fixe qui laisse chaque scène se dérouler en un seul plan ininterrompu, voici les ingrédients qui participent de la beauté d''Annie'", écrit le jury.
Série suisse

Enfin, la série documentaire "Le faiseur d'anges" de la Zurichoise Marina Klauser, qui raconte les abus sexuels subis dans la communauté religieuse bernoise Methernitha, remporte le prix "Swiss Series Storytelling Award". Le jury salue particulièrement la force du langage cinématographique et l'utilisation des métaphores visuelles.

Le GIFF a présenté 113 œuvres, dont 15 suisses. Le festival s'achève sur une fréquentation très réjouissante, selon les organisateurs et organisatrices, avec de nombreuses séances complètes et une nette augmentation des recettes de la billetterie, qui affiche une hausse de 30%, probablement favorisée par la baisse des tarifs d'entrée.

items.titel: SABO Project "softens divisions" inside Manhattan apartment
items.anriss: New York and Paris design studio SABO Project has introduced rounded partitions and bold green accents to a compact apartment on Manhattan's Lower East Side .

absaetze.t: New York and Paris design studio SABO Project has introduced rounded partitions and bold green accents to a compact apartment on Manhattan’s Lower East Side.
The 728-square-foot (68-square-metre) residence was renovated for a family of three with the help of contractor Alexar Interiors.
SABO Project opened up the plan and rounded the corners of walls and partitions between the various functional areas to visually improve the flow.
“The design aims to soften divisions between spaces so the apartment is experienced as a central living room extending into surrounding alcoves,” said the studio.
The apartment carries an industrial aesthetic thanks to exposed breeze-block walls, metal ductwork, concrete ceiling and polished concrete flooring.
Steel structural beams are painted a shade of mid green that is also applied to the lower kitchen cabinets, and appears on curtains and in artwork around the home.

“The apartment balances the rough materiality of exposed masonry blocks and ductwork with the soft textures of bespoke curtains, shades, and rugs,” said SABO Project. “Bold graphic forms animate curtains designed for each room.”
In the open-plan living area, a circular rug in the centre is mirrored on the ceiling by a white-painted circle that’s crossed with a minimalist light fixture.
Along one wall, stacks of concrete blocks with arch-shaped openings form a bench and a display console, accompanied at one end by a small wooden table.
“A long bench runs from the main room into a small outdoor space, conceived as an interior and enclosed with light-filtering fabric and a delicate steel mesh,” said the studio.
This small sun room is accessed via sliding glass doors from the living area and is also visible from the kitchen through a fixed glazed panel.
Here, green outdoor furniture from the Bouroullec brothers’ Palissade collection offers additional seating alongside the breeze-block bench.
Two identically sized bedrooms – one for the parents and another for their child – are decorated with the same colour and material palette as the rest of the apartment.
Quartets of breeze blocks are stacked on their sides to form nightstands with cubbies, and green appears again in the bedding.
In the bathroom, white tiles with green grout get progressively smaller as they reach the ceiling, creating a subtle gradient effect through density.
A lozenge-shaped mirror and sconce, and a basin with filleted corners continue the rounded forms found throughout the residence.
SABO Project was founded by architect Alexandre Delaunay, who works between New York and Paris on a range of residential, commercial and cultural projects.

The studio’s portfolio includes a Brooklyn loft featuring an irregular clustered storage unit, a Parisian apartment with multicoloured flooring and space-saving stairs, and another residence in the French capital that includes peg-hole walls and a curved child-proof staircase.
Photography by Alexandre Delaunay

items.titel: Archéologie : « Une découverte exceptionnelle » en Bavière, la riche tombe d’une femme celte révèle une surprenante offrande funéraire

absaetze.t: Lors de fouilles préventives menées à Senden en Allemagne, des archéologues ont découvert une tombe de l’âge du Fer vieille de 2300 ans. Cette sépulture remarquable renfermait la dépouille d’une femme celte, parée de précieux bijoux en bronze et accompagnée d’une étonnante offrande alimentaire.

Présentée durant le congrès annuel consacré à l’« Archéologie en Bavière » des 30 octobre et 1er novembre derniers, cette tombe du second âge du Fer (450 à 50 av. J.-C.) révèle des pratiques funéraires méconnues du monde celtique. Les fouilles menées en 2024 à Senden, dans le sud-ouest de l’Allemagne, ont permis aux chercheurs de mettre au jour les restes d’une femme celte portant des bracelets à nœuds et des anneaux de jambe en bronze et en sapropélite. Fait relativement rare : elle renfermait également les ossements d’un agneau ou d’un chevreau, déposés en tant qu’offrande alimentaire aux côtés de la défunte. Cette découverte exceptionnelle soulève de nouveaux questionnements sur les croyances religieuses, les rites funéraires et les relations sociales à l’époque de La Tène en Bavière.
Une tombe de l’Âge du Fer découverte par hasard en Bavière

Tout commence en 2024, lors d’une opération de sauvetage menée sur le site d’une future zone d’activités dans la rue Saint-Florian à Senden, en Bavière (arrondissement de Neu-Ulm). Les fouilleurs de l’Office régional bavarois pour la conservation des monuments historiques (Bayerisches Landesamt für Denkmalpflege [BLfD]) découvrent plusieurs vestiges : des sépultures de l’époque romaine et de la période mérovingienne, ainsi qu’un vaste habitat du haut Moyen Âge.
La tombe d’une femme inconnue à Senden en Allemagne. Credit: Dr. Matthias Leicht/Archäologie Dr. Arnolds & Kollegen GbR.

La mise au jour d’une riche tombe du second âge du Fer (période de La Tène), renfermant les restes d’une femme celte inhumée vers 250 av. J.-C., est donc une véritable surprise ! D’après l’étude anthropologique, la défunte serait décédée entre 40 et 60 ans. Le Dr Stefanie Berg, responsable du département d’archéologie du BLfD, explique le contexte de cette découverte : « La tombe de femme découverte à Senden représente une découverte exceptionnelle, qui s’inscrit dans une histoire bien plus vaste : sur le site des fouilles, nous avons mis en évidence des traces d’occupation allant de l’époque celtique à la période impériale romaine. De tels vestiges démontrent de manière frappante que cette région a constitué un espace de peuplement intensément occupé au fil des millénaires. »
Le contenu de la tombe celte de Senden
Une femme celte parée de bijoux en bronze et en sapropélite

Durant la fouille de la tombe, les archéologues ont exhumé une série de bijoux en bronze qui ornaient la dépouille de la défunte. Deux imposants anneaux à nœuds étaient placés autour de ses chevilles, tandis que ses bras et ses poignets étaient parés de deux bracelets à nœuds plus fins et d’un anneau à bossage creux équipé d’un ingénieux système de fermeture. À l’intérieur de l’un d’eux, les chercheurs ont trouvé un minuscule fragment de textile, dont l’étude pourrait apporter de précieuses informations sur les techniques de tissage de l’époque.
Les deux anneaux déposés comme offrandes dans la tombe. Credit: BLfD

Ces parures annulaires caractéristiques du second âge du Fer étaient accompagnées d’une broche en bronze et d’un bracelet lisse en sapropélite, une roche sédimentaire organique fossilisée provenant sans doute de Bohême. Elles témoignaient vraisemblablement de la richesse de l’individu qui les portait et pourraient indiquer que cette femme celte jouissait d’un certain statut social au sein de sa communauté.

De telles sépultures restent relativement rares en Bavière. À ce jour, une centaine de tombes de La Tène sont répertoriées dans la région. La tombe celtique de Senden révèle que l’inhumation de la défunte a été réalisée avec le plus grand soin, en veillant à la parer d’une riche panoplie de bijoux.
Un des objets retrouvés dans la tombe de Senden. Credit: BLfD.
Une étonnante offrande alimentaire

Les fouilleurs n’étaient toutefois pas au bout de leurs surprises ! La sépulture renfermait également les restes d’un petit animal, placé près de la hanche de la défunte. D’après le Dr Matthias Leicht, directeur d’opération chez ADA — Archäologie GbR, il s’agirait d’un agneau ou d’un chevreau. Cette étonnante découverte pourrait correspondre à une offrande alimentaire ou rituelle, effectuée au moment des funérailles. Une autre hypothèse serait que ce dépôt indique un lien personnel entre l’animal et cette femme celte.

Près de 2300 ans après sa mise en œuvre, la tombe celte de Senden amène les archéologues à s’interroger sur les pratiques funéraires et les croyances religieuses des communautés de l’Âge du Fer en Bavière. La présentation de cette découverte à l’occasion du colloque annuel organisé par le BLfD et la Société d’archéologie de Bavière a permis aux spécialistes d’ouvrir de nouvelles pistes de réflexion, tout en sensibilisant le grand public à la préservation du patrimoine archéologique régional.
Un des objets retrouvés dans la tombe de Senden. Credit: BLfD
